extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, and methodologists studying peer review reliability and meta-analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical findings for measuring, meta-analysing, and interpreting inter-rater reliability (IRR) of journal peer reviews, and for design/reporting decisions that affect IRR estimates. Focuses on quantitative meta-analysis methods and covariates that explain variation in reported reliabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-rater reliability (IRR) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: IRR is defined as 'the extent to which two or more independent reviews of the same scientific document agree' (Cicchetti).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the central quantity of interest in studies of peer review; IRR captures agreement among reviewers' ratings of the same manuscript. Low IRR indicates substantial disagreement among reviewers and is a key weakness of peer review processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: IRR measurement metrics (Cohen's Kappa, ICC, Pearson r)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nearly all studies provided the following quantitative IRR coefficients: Cohen's Kappa, intra-class correlation (ICC), and Pearson product-moment correlation (r).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meta-analyses can combine these metrics but must account for differences in scale and interpretation. The paper reports mean ICC/r ≈ .34 (random effects) and mean Cohen's Kappa ≈ .17, illustrating generally low IRR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for ICC (and handling of r/Kappa)
rubrics_metrics.description: If different coefficients were reported for the same sample, ICCs were included in the meta-analyses (n=35). If there were no ICCs available, r (n=9) or Cohen's Kappa (n=26) was used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICC measures absolute consensus and consistency and is preferable when available. r can overestimate IRR unless reviewers have identical means and variances; to include ICC and r in one analysis, use the square root of the ICC as a correlation analogue and apply Fisher Z-transformations to correlations and corresponding standard errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample size (number of manuscripts) as a covariate
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of manuscripts used to calculate reliability coefficients was used as a covariate (divided by 100 for interpretability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Larger sample sizes are associated with smaller reported IRR coefficients (regression coefficient ≈ −.03 per 100 manuscripts). This reflects publication bias: small studies tend to be published only if they report high IRR. Include sample size as a covariate in meta-analyses and be wary of small-sample inflated estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method used to calculate IRR (ICC vs r) as covariate
rubrics_metrics.description: Method used for calculation of the IRR (ICC or r) was included because inter-rater reliabilities vary considerably depending on computation method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect different magnitudes by method; r can considerably overestimate IRR except in special cases. When combining methods, transform measures appropriately (e.g., sqrt(ICC), Fisher Z) and test method effects in meta-regression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline (field) as covariate
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific discipline was coded (economics/law; natural sciences; medical sciences; social sciences) to test whether discipline influences IRR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theoretical expectations (more agreement in natural/physical sciences) exist, but this study found no significant discipline effect. Still, include discipline as a possible explanatory covariate and dummy-code categorical disciplines, treating missing values as 'unknown' to preserve power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object of appraisal (abstracts vs full papers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Object of appraisal (e.g., abstracts submitted to conferences vs papers submitted to journals) was included as a covariate because object type may influence IRR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstracts may lead to higher reviewer disagreement because they offer abbreviated information; expect variation by object and include this factor in analyses of IRR differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohort (time period) as covariate
rubrics_metrics.description: Cohort (the period on which a study's data is based, coded into time categories) was used to test whether IRR levels have changed over time (since 1950).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include cohort/time-period coding to examine temporal trends in IRR; code categories and handle missings to maintain analytic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blinding (single vs double) as covariate
rubrics_metrics.description: Type of blinding (single-blind, double-blind) was tested to see if masking author identity influences IRR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although double-blinding is intended to reduce bias, this meta-analysis found no significant effect on IRR—masking is often imperfect (reviewers may infer author identity). Nonetheless, report blinding type and test its effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rating system (reported or not; metric vs categorical; number of points)
rubrics_metrics.description: Type of rating system used by reviewers (metric or categorical, and whether reported) was included as a covariate. Some studies did not report rating-system details (coded as 'unknown').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting the rating system was associated with smaller reported IRR; failure to report is an indicator of lower study quality and can bias results. Prior work showed reliability increases with more rating-scale points. Authors should describe evaluation sheets/rating systems in detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of reviewers / reader system
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence suggests using more reviewers (e.g., three or four) or a 'reader system' where expert readers rate all proposals can increase IRR substantially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neff & Olden and Marsh et al. showed 3–4 reviewers or dedicated reader trials greatly improve single-rater reliability (reader system IRR up to ~.88). Consider increasing reviewer numbers or adopting reader systems to improve reliability, balanced against cost and desired diversity of perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multilevel (three-level) modelling to account for dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: Multilevel models (three-level: manuscript, sample, study) are used to estimate overall reliability and between-study variability while accounting for non-independence of multiple coefficients from the same study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multilevel models are preferred over simple fixed- or random-effects because they model dependency among effect sizes (e.g., multiple samples within a study) and provide better estimates of variance components; use recommended syntax/tools (e.g., SAS PROC MIXED) and impute within-study standard errors into level-1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed effects vs random effects models (conceptual choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixed effects assume the IRR in the population is the same for all studies (variability due only to sampling error); random effects estimate the average of a distribution of reliabilities and incorporate between-study variability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose model based on whether you wish to generalize to included studies only (fixed) or to a super-population of studies (random). Use Q tests to assess heterogeneity; if heterogeneity exists, random effects or multilevel models are preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-regression to explain heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is high between-study variation, meta-regression analyses using covariates (e.g., sample size, method, discipline) should be calculated to explain heterogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dummy-code categorical covariates, handle missing values as an 'unknown' category to retain power, and ensure sufficient studies per covariate (authors followed a rule-of-thumb recommending enough studies to support models with two or more covariates). Compare models with loglikelihood and BIC; include only significant covariates in final models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion criteria for meta-analysis (must report coefficient and sample size)
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies were eligible only if they reported the reliability coefficient (ICC, r, or Cohen's Kappa) and the number of manuscripts; 52 of 84 located studies reported the information required, and ultimately 48 studies were included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For meta-analytic inclusion, ensure primary studies report both the IRR metric and sample size (or information to compute standard errors). Studies lacking these data cannot be meta-analysed and should be excluded or treated separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighting by standard error and use of Fisher Z / Bayes estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Meta-analyses weight studies by the inverse of the standard error of the IRR estimate. Fisher Z-transformations were applied to correlations and standard errors; predicted coefficients are Bayes estimates that account for sampling error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smaller standard errors (larger samples) receive greater weight. Apply Fisher Z-transform to correlations for approximate normality and compute/transform back for interpretation. Empirical Bayes shrinkage pulls imprecise small-sample estimates toward the overall mean.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation benchmarks (Landis & Koch for Kappa)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean Cohen's Kappa amounting to .17 was interpreted using Landis and Koch guidelines as indicating 'slight' IRR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting Kappa, refer to established interpretation guidelines (e.g., Landis & Koch) but apply caution: contextualize with sample size and study design; Kappa near .17 indicates slight agreement beyond chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication bias / file-drawer problem awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication bias is the tendency to submit or accept manuscripts based on the direction or strength of findings; studies with small samples appear published only when reporting high IRR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test for publication bias (e.g., examine relationship between sample size and reported effect). Recognize that high reported IRR from small studies may be less credible. Adjust meta-analytic interpretation accordingly and include sample size as covariate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting standards recommendation (describe evaluation sheet/rating system)
rubrics_metrics.description: Future primary studies on IRR should be based on large sample sizes and describe the evaluation sheet/rating system for reviewers in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoroughly report rating instruments, scale points, and operational definitions of judgments. Lack of such reporting is an indicator of low study quality and is associated with inflated IRR in this meta-analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat: high IRR may be less credible (small-sample effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies that report a high level of IRR are to be considered less credible than those with low IRR because high IRR coefficients are often based on small sample sizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret high IRR cautiously—check sample size and reporting quality. Prefer large-sample estimates weighted by standard error and validated rating systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for qualitative/in-depth studies on reviewer disagreement causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Very few studies investigated reviewer agreement with the purpose of identifying actual reasons behind reviewer disagreement; in-depth studies (e.g., content analyses of reviewers' comment sheets) are scarce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement quantitative IRR studies with qualitative analyses to explore how reviewers apply standards, differences in leniency/strictness, and the dislocational components of judgments. Such mixed methods can inform improvements to rating systems and reviewer training.
